doc.title: Christine Jensen interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 4, 2024

title: Life in the United States compared with Canada
summary: Asked about the U.S., she is worried but hopeful that music survives, and compares guns, health care and racial divides with Canada; mentions Tilting World.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: It’s been a fascinating conversation. I’m going to wrap up with — it’s not really a musical question but I’m curious, growing up to the north, in Canada, and then coming here, do you have an opinion or a sense of where the United States is currently?

That’s a terribly long horrible question. I’m very worried. At the same time I think some things will always survive. It’s kind of like watching Wall-E the movie and you see the little plant that survives through all of it. I feel like music is like that. It’s always going to be there. It’s always going to survive. And I hope that it gives good to people. Because there’s so much other stuff out there that’s not good, like crime. I moved here and I just went, “Oh yeah, guns?” Guns and Medicare. These are the two issues. And in fact guns are the top of the issue because they stem from all of the strife underneath it that is happening because of the erosion of simple things like — like in Canada you don’t spend your day talking about Medicare and going broke. You know what I mean? You don’t — that is just not a part of the conversation. Okay we’ve gotten rid of something that takes up a lot of time and money and now we can focus on other things. Not that Canada is the perfect place because it certainly isn’t. There’s a whole bunch of underlying things with social medical systems right now especially. The economy is still a problem. Here I think there’s a different focus on racial divide. Canada has a lot of issues they’ve never worked on. They just didn’t have to deal with it the way the United States — they would have if they had more migration up there. And there is some, but it’s not at the level of what happened in the States with the red line and with economic disparity amongst race. It’s just so wrong. So I’m here dealing with all this as a institution of privilege really, but hope that I do think that the positive thing is that we’re all at least facing the demons I’m talking about and trying to find other solutions. It’s going to be hard. It’s going to take a lot of like really breaking some tradition that has been in the hands of the privileged. I don’t know what it is and I don’t know how it will happen because the government coming in — just like in Canada — it’s going to slash anything to do with the arts because the arts are a voice for political movement.
You’ve given us a lot to think about.
I hope I said that okay but I’m just like —
You said it’s a long and terrible question. It’s terrible that we have to even ask it, but I appreciate your thoughts today, and — very illuminating.

Yeah. And I think the whole world, again, I wrote a piece for Ryan Truesdell, he did a string project and it’s called “Tilting World.” And I really feel like the world did somewhere tilt in the pandemic because that’s — it just shook everything up and now we have to deal with things.
